summary:
This evaluation covered 7 eval scenarios (36 iterations total, no runs failed). Two of the seven ("negative-sibling-boundary" and "negative-unrelated") were negative/no-trigger tests where expected_output, assertions, metrics, comparison, and consistency were all marked skipped by design (should_trigger: false) — both variants correctly did not fire in those cases, so they contribute no comparative signal and are not counted against either variant.

Across the five remaining evals (mlv-pipelines-locked, mlv-fillmsec, mlv-recovering, mlv-alert-paths, mlv-inputloss-scope), the trigger fired 100% of the time for both variants in all cases. The clearest and most consistent pattern is on "expected_output" and per-assertion pass rates: with_skill met the expected output in all 3/3 runs for every one of these five evals (100%), while without_skill's expected-output pass rate was markedly lower and varied by eval — 1/3 (mlv-pipelines-locked), 0/3 (mlv-fillmsec, mlv-recovering, mlv-alert-paths, mlv-inputloss-scope). Confidence on these expected-output judgments was rated "high" throughout, so this is not a low-confidence artifact. At the assertion level, with_skill passed all assertions (100%) in every eval, while without_skill's assertion pass rates ranged from 88% (pipelines-locked) down to 0% (recovering, alert-paths, inputloss-scope) and 22% (fillmsec). Some individual assertions (e.g., simple keyword regex checks like mentioning 'HLS' or 'sync'/'diverged' in mlv-pipelines-locked) passed for both variants ("always_passes" pattern) and thus don't differentiate them, but most assertions in the other four evals followed a "with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails" pattern, and a few were flagged "flaky" (e.g., the 60,000ms-cap mention in mlv-fillmsec), indicating some inconsistency in without_skill's phrasing across runs rather than a uniform failure mode.

On runtime and cost, with_skill was consistently faster and cheaper (e.g., 3-4s / $0.03-0.04 per eval) while without_skill took noticeably longer and cost more in every eval (16-19s/$0.14-0.16 for pipelines-locked and fillmsec, 48s/$0.40 for recovering, and up to 1m1s/$0.51 for inputloss-scope). Output consistency (run-to-run stability) favored with_skill in most evals — rated "consistent" (score 3.0) in three evals and "mostly_consistent" in two — while without_skill ranged from "mostly_consistent" to "inconsistent" (e.g., score 1.33 in mlv-fillmsec), suggesting without_skill's outputs varied more across repeated runs in some scenarios. One eval (mlv-alert-paths) showed equal consistency scores (2.67) for both variants.

Direct quality-comparison data (head-to-head LLM judging) was mostly unavailable: in four of the five evals all quality-comparison pairs were skipped (0 pairs evaluated), and in the remaining eval (mlv-pipelines-locked) only 1 of 3 pairs could be evaluated, with that limited sample favoring without_skill on accuracy/completeness and with_skill on actionability, at only medium confidence — too sparse to draw a firm conclusion.

Taken together, across these five evals with_skill showed higher and more consistent expected-output/assertion pass rates, faster runtime, lower cost, and more stable repeated outputs, while without_skill showed higher runtime/cost and lower, more variable pass rates and consistency. However, genuine head-to-head quality judgments are largely missing data (mostly skipped), so this picture rests heavily on expected-output/assertion pass rates and consistency metrics rather than on direct quality comparison.

mlv-pipelines-locked.summary:
Both variants were triggered consistently (3/3), so the behavior under test fired reliably in all runs for both.

Expected-output match: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in only 1 of 3 runs (33%, high confidence). This is the clearest and most consistent signal in the data — confidence in the expected-output judgments is high for both, so this gap is not an artifact of weak measurement.

Per-assertion detail: with_skill passed all 12 assertion checks (12/12), while without_skill passed 7/8 (88%). Looking at individual assertions, three (mentioning "sync"/"diverged", "HLS", "UDP") passed 100% for both variants — these are not differentiating anything, since both systems satisfy them easily. The one assertion that does differentiate is the more substantive LLM-graded check (naming the eligible pipeline pair as out of sync and naming all four specific output groups: HLS, MediaPackage, MS Smooth, UDP) — with_skill passed this 3/3, while without_skill passed only 1/2 (it was marked "flaky" for without_skill, and note without_skill only had 2 scored instances here versus 3 for with_skill, so this is a smaller sample).

Quality comparison: only 1 of 3 pairs could actually be compared (2 were skipped), so this dimension rests on very little data. In that single comparable pair, per-criterion results split: without_skill was favored on accuracy and completeness, with_skill was favored on actionability. Overall across the (limited) quality judgments, without_skill was favored 2 times and with_skill 1 time, at medium confidence — a thin, mixed signal given the small sample.

Runtime and cost: with_skill was notably faster (~4s avg) and cheaper (~$0.03) than without_skill (~16s avg, ~$0.14). Neither exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the one pair evaluated for that comparison.

Output consistency: with_skill's outputs were rated fully consistent across repeated runs (score 3.0, high confidence). No consistency rating is available for without_skill (null), so no comparison can be made on this dimension — it's simply missing data for without_skill, not a sign of inconsistency.

Overall picture: with_skill met the expected output and the harder assertion more reliably across runs, and did so faster and cheaper, with confirmed run-to-run consistency. without_skill's shortfall on expected-output matching and the detailed assertion is a real, high-confidence-measured gap, but the limited quality comparison (only 1 of 3 pairs usable) leaned slightly toward without_skill on accuracy/completeness for the one response it was judged on, and without_skill's own consistency across runs is unmeasured. These quality and consistency gaps mean the picture isn't fully one-sided, but the expected-output and assertion data are the most robust findings here.

mlv-fillmsec.summary:
This eval tested a chat task about a MediaLive encoding timing issue (60,000 ms cap, PTS/GOP timing or scheduled input switch). The trigger behavior fired in all 3 runs (this fact was only measured in aggregate, not per-variant).

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, high confidence), while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (high confidence). This is a clear, high-confidence divergence rather than a borderline call.

Assertions: with_skill passed all 9/9 assertion checks (100%), while without_skill passed only 2/9 (22%). Breaking this down by the three distinct assertions: the LLM-judged assertion about stating the 60,000 ms cap and pointing to encoding/timing causes passed consistently for with_skill (3/3) and failed consistently for without_skill (0/3) — a clear split. The two regex-based assertions (checking for mention of "60,000"/"60000" and "PTS"/"timing"/"GOP") were flaky for without_skill, each passing only 1/3 runs, while passing 3/3 for with_skill. No assertion passed for neither variant, and none passed equally for both, so these checks are meaningfully differentiating.

Metrics: with_skill was notably faster (3s avg vs 19s avg) and cheaper ($0.03 vs $0.16 avg) than without_skill. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.6% vs 3.9%), with no compaction needed in either case.

Quality comparison: no head-to-head quality pairs could be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no direct quality-comparison data to weigh here — this dimension is absent rather than neutral.

Output consistency: with_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.67, high confidence), while without_skill was rated "inconsistent" (score 1.33, high confidence), aligning with the flaky regex assertion results for without_skill — its outputs varied more across repeated runs.

Overall, across expected-output match, assertion pass rates, runtime, cost, and consistency, with_skill showed uniformly stronger and more stable results in this single eval, with all measurements at high confidence. However, this is based on only 3 runs per variant for one eval, and no comparative quality-judgment data was available, so the breadth of evidence is limited despite the consistency of the signal within it.

mlv-recovering.summary:
This single chat-task eval (AWS Elemental MediaLive, Operations/Observability, CHAT/INCIDENT_RCA context) tested whether the agent's response correctly explains automatic pipeline restart behavior and recommends escalation when a RECOVERING state persists beyond 5 minutes.

Trigger behavior: the scenario-under-test fired in all 3/3 runs, so the comparison data is based on a full, valid sample.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 3/3 runs (100%), while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (0%). Both measurements were rated with high confidence, so this is not a low-certainty finding — it reflects a consistent, clearly-judged difference.

Assertions: there were two underlying checks (one LLM-graded, one regex-based), both applied 3 times each (6 total per variant). Both assertions passed 6/6 for with_skill and failed 6/6 (0/6) for without_skill. Notably, these are the same two assertions each time, not six independent checks, and both show the identical pattern (with_skill passes, without_skill fails) — meaning there's no case here of an assertion passing for both, failing for both, or splitting in the opposite direction. This is a consistent, repeated signal within this one eval rather than many corroborating independent measurements.

Quality comparison: no side-by-side quality pairs were actually evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no quality-preference data to weigh here — this dimension is absent, not neutral or tied.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged ~4s and $0.04 per run, while without_skill averaged ~48s and $0.40 per run — without_skill took about 12x longer and cost about 10x more. Context window utilization was nearly identical (~4.5-4.6%) with no compaction for either.

Output consistency: with_skill's outputs were rated fully "consistent" across runs (score 3.0, high confidence). without_skill was rated "mostly consistent" (score 2.33, medium confidence), indicating somewhat more run-to-run variation and a weaker confidence basis for that consistency judgment.

Overall state: across every measured dimension in this eval — expected-output success, assertion pass rate, runtime, cost, and consistency — with_skill's results were stronger, and none of the measurements here show an offsetting advantage for without_skill (e.g., no quality-preference data exists to suggest without_skill's extra time/cost bought better output). This is a case where the dimensions point in the same direction rather than presenting a tradeoff, though it rests on a small sample (3 runs) for a single eval, and the quality-comparison dimension that might have revealed a nuance was skipped entirely.

mlv-alert-paths.summary:
This eval tested a chat task around AWS Elemental MediaLive alerting (expecting mention of the ListAlerts API, encoder logs, and EventBridge MediaLive Channel Alert events). The trigger for the test fired in all 3 runs, so the behavior under test was reliably exercised.

On expected output and assertions, there is a clear, consistent split: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, high confidence) and passed all 12 assertion checks (12/12, 100%), while without_skill failed to meet the expected output in any run (0/3) and failed all 12 assertions (0/12). This pattern is uniform across every individual assertion (naming the ListAlerts API, mentioning encoder logs, mentioning EventBridge, and the regex check for 'list-alerts'/'ListAlerts') — there is no assertion where results were mixed or where both variants struggled equally; with_skill passed everything checked and without_skill passed nothing checked. Confidence in these judgments is high for both variants, so this is not a low-confidence artifact.

Quality comparison data is not available: all 3 pairs were skipped and none were evaluated, so no direct quality judgment can be drawn beyond the assertion/expected-output results.

On efficiency, with_skill was faster (avg 3s vs 7s) and cheaper (avg $0.03 vs $0.06) than without_skill, though both runtimes and costs are low in absolute terms and context window utilization was nearly identical (~4.6-4.7%) with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency across repeated runs was essentially identical for both variants: each was rated 'mostly_consistent' overall with the same score (2.67) and the same dimension split (2 consistent, 1 mostly consistent), with high confidence. So neither variant showed a stability problem relative to the other.

Overall, the dimensions point in a consistent direction for this eval: with_skill satisfied the expected content and all assertions while without_skill did not satisfy any of them, and with_skill also ran faster and cheaper. However, this is based on a single eval with only 3 runs, and no comparative quality-judgment data was available (all pairs skipped) to independently corroborate the content difference beyond the assertion checks themselves.

mlv-inputloss-scope.summary:
This single chat-task eval tested whether the agent correctly explains that InputLossSeconds only applies to RTP Push and MediaConnect inputs (and that for other input types, NetworkIn = 0 and InputVideoFrameRate = 0 should be used instead).

Trigger: the behavior under test fired in all 3 runs (3/3), so the scenario was exercised as intended for both variants.

Expected output / assertions: There is a stark, consistent split here. with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, high confidence) and passed both underlying assertions (the LLM-judged explanation assertion and the regex check for "NetworkIn") in every run (6/6 assertions overall). without_skill failed the expected output in all 3 runs (0/3, high confidence) and failed both assertions in every run (0/6). Confidence in these judgments is high on both sides, so this is not a borderline or noisy measurement — it reflects a real, repeatable behavioral difference on this specific task, with one assertion passing for both variants nowhere and one failing for both nowhere (both assertions show the exact same with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails pattern, so they're aligned rather than contradictory).

Quality comparison: No side-by-side quality pairs were actually evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there's no independent quality signal beyond the assertion/expected-output results — this dimension is effectively missing data here, not a tie.

Runtime and cost: with_skill was notably faster (~3s avg) and cheaper (~$0.03) than without_skill (~1m1s avg, ~$0.51). Context window utilization was nearly identical (~4.6% vs 4.5%, no compaction for either), so this cost/time gap isn't explained by context size.

Output consistency: Both variants were fairly stable across repeated runs — with_skill was rated fully "consistent" (score 3.0), without_skill was "mostly consistent" (score 2.67, one dimension only mostly consistent rather than fully) — a small difference, with high confidence in both ratings.
